Set $v=u-1$. Then $v\in C^\infty(\overline\Omega)$ satisfies
$$\Delta v=-\lambda(v+1)\quad\text{in }\Omega,\qquad v=\partial_\nu v=0\quad\text{on }\partial\Omega.$$
Since $u$ is constant on $\partial\Omega$, the tangential derivatives vanish there, so the Neumann condition $\partial_\nu u=0$ actually gives $\nabla u=0$ on $\partial\Omega$, hence the Cauchy data $(0,0)$ for $v$ on the whole boundary.

This is the classical overdetermined problem studied by Serrin (1971). By the moving-plane method, any bounded smooth domain admitting a solution to $\Delta v=f(v)$ with $v=\partial_\nu v=0$ on $\partial\Omega$ and $f$ Lipschitz must be a Euclidean ball; here $f(v)=-\lambda(v+1)$ is Lipschitz. Equivalently, this is Schiffer's problem (version B), whose only smooth solutions are disks. Because the hypothesis explicitly excludes Euclidean disks, no admissible domain exists for any integer $N\ge2$. Thus $\mathcal A=\varnothing$ and
$$\sup\bigl(\{0\}\cup\mathcal A\bigr)=0.$$
